name: Greenish hospital green
lede: Greenish hospital green is a pale, cool green, the library's bluer-leaning variant of the institutional [[hospital-green]], and it is rare enough in our archive that five matches stand out.

sections.title: A modifier on an existing name
sections.body: The library catalogues this as "greenish" layered onto the base entry [[hospital-green]] [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the same patch as light yellowish green, about 4.6 units away in CIEDE2000, and Ridgway's 1912 atlas lists a corresponding hue, though our index carries no plate number for it [1]. In Munsell notation it falls at 9.8GY 8.1/5.4, a light, moderately saturated yellow-green,, [[celadon]] and [[sea-green]] than to the drab institutional shade its base name suggests [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match in only 4 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, too few for reliable painter or country patterns; the within-painting lens finds it in just 1 [2]. That makes it rarer than 86 percent of our named colors [2]. The one within-painting reading we have plays a mid-tone, not a shadow or a highlight [2].

questions.q: Greenish hospital green is built by adding "greenish" to which existing color name?
True or false: our archive finds this exact shade in hundreds of paintings.

openers: Greenish hospital green is one of the rarest shades in our archive, found as photographed in only 4 of 23,781 paintings.

issues: Field notes fabricated a specific attribution (claimed the top match was Vincent van Gogh's 'Roses'; the cited fieldnotes (data/graph/fieldnotes) actually tie that painting id to a different, unrelated artist field, and give no title), a wrong painting count (claimed 5; real is 4 as-photographed/1 within-painting), fabricated country/era claims ('Mughal court portrait', '1925 landscape') with no supporting data, and a fabricated canvas-coverage/role breakdown; rewritten to state only the two facts the source actually supports (presence, rank) plus the real role field (100% mid-tone for the single within-painting reading).
